cases.name: mint-default-jwt-ec
cases.note: The JOSE baseline: the policy floor profile over an EC signature. Every other JWT row is read against this one.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-rsa
cases.note: The same claims under RS512 — an RSA `alg`, a 512-byte signature, and a deterministic one.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-okp
cases.note: EdDSA over Ed25519 — the OKP header shape, and the smallest deterministic signature aegis emits.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-oct
cases.note: HS256 — the symmetric header shape on the JOSE wire, which no profile with an algClass floor can reach.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-akp
cases.note: ML-DSA-65 — the post-quantum header shape and the largest signature in the corpus.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-empty-claims
cases.note: The registry's empty-claim decision on the JOSE wire: the empty `nonce` is pruned and the empty `scope` is kept, with nothing asked for. A flipped `whenEmpty` cell shows here as a claims-bytes diff.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-typ
cases.note: An explicit `typ` overriding a profile that mandates none — the JOSE header type knob.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-header-bag
cases.note: The caller header bag on the JOSE wire: `objectId` becomes `oid`, `contentType` becomes `cty`.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-header-jwks-uri
cases.note: A caller `jwksUri` on a key that publishes its own: the kit's value is a DEFAULT, so `jku` on the wire is the caller's, not the key's.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-lifetime
cases.note: A per-call lifetime overriding the profile default — the `exp` claim, and nothing else, moves.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-structured-claims
cases.note: Every structured claim on the JOSE wire — `cnf`, a recursive `act`, `may_act`, `sub_id`, `events`, `authorization_details` and the nested `address`. It is the JOSE half of the pair: the domain↔JOSE translator shapes these, and its output is what the COSE byte layer then re-shapes, so a change that moved only one of the two shows on exactly one row.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-confirmation-thumbprint
cases.note: A confirmation member the COSE wire cannot carry: the registry marks `jkt` absent on COSE, so this row records the JOSE spelling of a member that has no COSE twin — the shared structured row deliberately does not carry it. RFC 9449 §6, RFC 7638.

cases.name: mint-default-jwt-hash-claims
cases.note: The three OIDC hashes on the JOSE wire, where each is the base64url string verbatim. Their COSE twin decodes that alphabet to bytes, so this row is what says which of the two the JOSE wire holds.

cases.name: mint-access-token-jwt-ec
cases.note: RFC 9068 access token — the `application/at+jwt` typ and the profile's own required claim set.

cases.name: mint-access-token-jwt-cert-thumbprint
cases.note: Cert binding, thumbprint mode — `x5t#S256` and its `x5t` companion on the protected header.

cases.name: mint-access-token-jwt-cert-chain
cases.note: Cert binding, chain mode — the whole `x5c` chain on the wire, beside both digests.

cases.name: mint-id-token-jwt-ec
cases.note: OIDC id token — the bare `JWT` typ, and a profile whose token id is NOT auto-injected but is still stamped when stated.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: mint-id-token-jwt-encrypted-rsa
cases.note: Sign-then-encrypt on the JOSE wire with RSA-OAEP-256 key wrapping — the one JWE in the corpus whose encrypted-key segment is non-empty.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: mint-id-token-jwt-encrypted-ecdh
cases.note: Sign-then-encrypt with ECDH-ES over P-521 — the ephemeral `epk` on the protected header and an empty encrypted-key segment.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: mint-id-token-jwt-encrypted-dir
cases.note: Sign-then-encrypt with a direct AES key — no key management on the wire at all, so only the IV, ciphertext and tag move.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-ec
cases.note: The COSE baseline: the same claims as the JOSE baseline, so the two wires can be read side by side.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-rsa
cases.note: RS512 on the COSE wire — a deterministic signature, so this row's token bytes are captured verbatim.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-okp
cases.note: EdDSA on the COSE wire — COSE label -8, whose curve is resolved from the key rather than the label.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-akp
cases.note: ML-DSA-65 on the COSE wire — RFC 9964 label -49.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-interoperable
cases.note: `proprietary: false` — the interop spelling, where a private-use claim label is written under its JOSE string key instead.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-proprietary
cases.note: The same content with the on-platform compact integer labels — the other half of the proprietary pair.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-header-bag
cases.note: The caller header bag on the COSE wire: the SAME domain option that produced `oid` on JOSE lands at the COSE label the parameter rides under. `oid` has no IANA COSE parameter, so it takes a lindorm PRIVATE-USE label — and this row states no `proprietary`, so aegis writes the INTEROPERABLE spelling, the text label `oid` rather than the private-use integer no foreign reader can interpret. The row below holds the other spelling. RFC 9052 §1.5, RFC 8152 §16.2.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-header-bag-proprietary
cases.note: The same header bag on-platform — the other half of the interop pair, and the only row that holds the private-use header label as an INTEGER. Without it the corpus would record one spelling of a parameter that has two, and a change that collapsed them back onto the compact form everywhere would move nothing here. `contentType` (label 3) is registered, so it is the integer in BOTH rows: the mode moves the private-use label and nothing else.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-empty-claims
cases.note: The same registry decision on the COSE wire — its own forward into the normalisation, so a prune that reached only one wire shows as a diff on exactly one of the two rows. The empty `amr` is the claim that carries it here: an empty text claim never reaches the CWT bytes anyway.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-structured-claims
cases.note: The same structured claims on the COSE wire, INTEROPERABLE. This is the row the CWT claim shaper writes: `cnf` becomes a COSE key map, and `act`/`may_act`/`sub_id` stay string-keyed because the compact form is on-platform only. A shaper that stopped shaping a claim would leave its JOSE-shaped value here and move exactly these bytes.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-structured-claims-proprietary
cases.note: The on-platform half of the pair — the same structured claims with the compact encodings turned on, so `act`/`may_act`/`sub_id` collapse from string-keyed maps to integer-labelled ones. Without this row the compact builders would have no wire record at all, and a shaper that stopped reaching them would move nothing.

cases.name: mint-default-cwt-hash-claims
cases.note: The three OIDC hashes on the COSE wire, where each is the BYTES the base64url string decodes to rather than the string itself. The JOSE twin holds the string, so the pair is what records that the two wires disagree deliberately.

cases.name: mint-access-token-cwt-ec
cases.note: RFC 9068 access token on the COSE wire — the `application/at+cwt` media type at COSE label 16.

cases.name: mint-id-token-cwt-ec
cases.note: The id token on the COSE wire — a profile whose JOSE typ is the bare `JWT` has to say something else here.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: mint-id-token-cwt-encrypted-dir
cases.note: Sign-then-encrypt on the COSE wire — a COSE_Encrypt0 whose IV rides the unprotected bucket (RFC 9052 §3.1).

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: mint-id-token-cwt-encrypted-gcm128
cases.note: The same wrapper under A128GCM — the content encryption is the one property of the resolved key legible from the protected bucket.

cases.name: mint-default-cwm-oct
cases.note: COSE_Mac0 — the symmetric COSE structure, which is a different tag chain from the signed one for the same claims.

cases.name: mint-id-token-cwm-oct
cases.note: A MACed id token in its COSE form — the HS-signed id token a confidential client may take. OIDC Core §10.1.

cases.name: mint-default-cwm-interoperable
cases.note: The interop label spelling on the MACed structure — `proprietary` is a claim-encoding knob, so it must reach cwm as well as cwt.

cases.name: sign-jws-object-ec
cases.note: An opaque JWS over a JSON object — no claims layer, so the payload bytes are the caller's own serialisation.

payload.reason: the payload is not JSON — it is an opaque JWS body

cases.name: sign-jws-string-okp
cases.note: An opaque JWS over a string — the payload passes through untouched, which is the property that separates `sign` from `mint`.

payload.reason: the payload is not JSON — it is an opaque JWS body

cases.name: sign-jws-bytes-oct
cases.note: An opaque JWS over raw bytes under HS256 — the payload segment is base64url of exactly those bytes.

cases.name: sign-jws-object-token-type
cases.note: The `tokenType` knob — the domain token type becomes the media type in the JOSE `typ` header.

cases.name: sign-jws-object-header-bag
cases.note: The caller header bag on the opaque JOSE path — the same translation the mint path performs, reached through a different door.

cases.name: sign-jws-object-cert
cases.note: Cert binding on the opaque JOSE path — the opaque JOSE namespace and `mint` resolve the binding through the same code, so both must be held. ⚠ `chain`, not `thumbprint`: a cert-bearing key emits `x5t#S256`/`x5t` on EVERY sign, so a `thumbprint` row produces bytes identical to a row that states nothing and the recorded token shows nothing about the option. `chain` is the only mode that adds `x5c` (RFC 7515 §4.1.6), so the recorded token is attributable to the request. ⚠ The corpus RECORDS; it does not assert header contents — the capability itself is held by the disposition probe row `jose signOpaque forwards bindCertificate`. The COSE twin honours `bindCertificate` too: `CwsKit.sign` resolves it and writes `x5chain` at label 33 (RFC 9360 §2).

payload.reason: the payload is not a CBOR map, so it carries no claims to read (it is not decodable CBOR)

cases.name: sign-cws-object-ec
cases.note: An opaque COSE_Sign1 over a JSON object — the CWS content codec stamps `application/json` and the payload stays a bstr.

payload.reason: the payload is not a CBOR map, so it carries no claims to read (it is not decodable CBOR)

cases.name: sign-cws-string-okp
cases.note: An opaque COSE_Sign1 over a string under a deterministic signature — this row's token bytes are captured verbatim.

payload.reason: the payload is not a CBOR map, so it carries no claims to read (it is not decodable CBOR)

cases.name: sign-cws-bytes-oct
cases.note: Raw bytes under a shared secret — a CWS with a symmetric key is a COSE_Mac0, not a COSE_Sign1.

payload.reason: the payload is not a CBOR map, so it carries no claims to read (it is not decodable CBOR)

cases.name: sign-cws-object-token-type
cases.note: The `tokenType` knob on the COSE wire — the same domain option produces a `+cws` media type here.

payload.reason: the payload is not a CBOR map, so it carries no claims to read (it is not decodable CBOR)

cases.name: sign-cws-object-header-bag
cases.note: The caller header bag on the opaque COSE path — the same parameter the JOSE twin writes, at the COSE label it rides under. `oid` is a lindorm PRIVATE-USE label and this row states no `proprietary`, so the interoperable spelling is on the wire: the text label `oid`, which every conformant COSE reader can parse, rather than the private-use integer only lindorm can interpret.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-rsa
cases.note: A domain-named object sealed to an RSA-OAEP-256 recipient — no inner signature, and a non-empty encrypted-key segment. The plaintext is the caller's own JSON, so `cty` is `application/json`.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-ecdh
cases.note: A domain-named object sealed under ECDH-ES over P-521 — the ephemeral key on the protected header.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-ecdh-party
cases.note: The ECDH-ES party info (RFC 7518 §4.6) — `apu`/`apv` are emitted AND fed to the KDF, so they change the header and the ciphertext together.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-okp-ecdh
cases.note: ECDH-ES over X25519 — an OKP ephemeral key, whose `epk` has no `y` member.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-opaque-string-dir
cases.note: An opaque string sealed with a direct key — the `cty` says `text/plain`, which is the read side's reconstruction cue.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-opaque-bytes-dir
cases.note: Opaque bytes sealed with a direct key — no `cty` interpretation at all, so the plaintext is returned as bytes.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-opaque-bytes-cbc
cases.note: AES-CBC-HMAC content encryption — a standard JOSE `enc` value, and private-use on COSE, so the same key is standard here and gated there. RFC 7518 §5.2.3, RFC 9053 §4.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-type
cases.note: The `type` knob — the domain token type becomes the JWE media type in `typ`.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-header-bag
cases.note: The caller header bag on the encrypt path — reaching the JWE writer, which is the only encrypt path that takes one.

payload.reason: a 5-part JWE carries ciphertext where a JWS carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-jwe-claims-cert
cases.note: Cert binding on a JWE — the recipient key carries a chain, so the thumbprint rides the protected header.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-claims-dir
cases.note: A domain-named object sealed as a COSE_Encrypt0 — the plaintext is the caller's own JSON under the caller's own keys, so `cty` (label 3) is `application/json`, the same answer every other opaque door gives. ⚠ It is NOT a CWT Claims Set: an encrypt has no signature behind it, so aegis may not promote `subject` to the registered label 2 a conformant reader would take for an asserted claim. Sealing a CWT is `mint(…, { encrypt })`, which signs first. RFC 8392 §4.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-claims-gcm128
cases.note: The same object under A128GCM — the protected bucket's content encryption is what tells the two recipient keys apart.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-claims-interoperable
cases.note: `proprietary: false` on the COSE seal — the interoperable default, stated. On this verb it reaches ONLY the encryption registration gate: there is no claim codec on the encrypt path any more, so the flag cannot move the plaintext, and this row is byte-comparable to `encrypt-cwe-claims-dir` for that reason rather than because false is the default. ⚠ THE CORPUS CANNOT SEE A PLAINTEXT AT ALL — it is ciphertext — so the flag's inability to reach it is pinned by `src/classes/cose-claims-encoding.test.ts#does not let proprietary reach the plaintext at all`, which decrypts and compares the bytes; this row holds the wire length steady around it.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-claims-cbc-proprietary
cases.note: AES-CBC-HMAC on the COSE wire — aegis emits it under a lindorm private-use label, so it is reachable only through the proprietary gate, which is the one thing that flag still decides here. RFC 9053 §4.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-opaque-bytes-dir
cases.note: Opaque bytes as a COSE_Encrypt0 — `cty` is `application/octet-stream` and the plaintext is returned as those bytes.

payload.reason: a COSE_Encrypt0 carries ciphertext where a COSE_Sign1/Mac0 carries its payload

cases.name: encrypt-cwe-opaque-string-type
cases.note: An opaque string with a caller `type` — the one place an opaque `cwe` carries a media type of the caller's choosing.
